name: PowerShell - TCP Port Scan One-Liner (TcpClient)
description: PowerShell one-liner that iterates a port range, attempts a .NET TcpClient connection on each, and prints 'TCP port N is open' for successful handshakes. No extra tools needed — pure .NET on any Windows host.
notes: 2>$null suppresses the connection-refused exceptions so only open ports print. New-Object Net.Sockets.TcpClient performs a full TCP connect (same as nmap -sT) — visible in PCAP as SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK sequences. Slow on large ranges because each attempt is sequential and synchronous. For faster scanning use the try/catch filter variation which skips the exception-printing overhead. Requires PowerShell 2+ (all modern Windows).

recommended.note: Test-NetConnection is cleaner for single-port checks and returns structured output.
nmap -sT is faster and provides service fingerprinting; use when nmap is available from Kali.

defense.prerequisites: Compromised Windows foothold with PowerShell access. No elevated privileges required.
defense.why_it_works: .NET's TcpClient.Connect() performs a full TCP three-way handshake. Success (port open) completes without exception; failure (closed or filtered) throws a SocketException, which 2>$null silences. The loop over a range gives sequential port coverage using only built-in .NET classes — no executable is written to disk.
defense.misconfiguration: Hosts with open ports not filtered by host-based firewall. PowerShell module/script-block logging not enabled. Lack of network IPS rules for sequential port probes.
defense.impact: Maps open TCP ports across a target host from a Windows foothold. Enables pivot planning — identify SMB (445), RDP (3389), WinRM (5985), SQL (1433) before launching targeted attacks.
defense.detection: PowerShell script block logging (Event 4104) captures the loop expression. Event 4688 (command-line auditing) shows powershell.exe arguments. Network: sequential TCP SYN packets from the foothold host to the target visible in PCAP and IPS logs. IDS rule: >50 SYN packets to distinct ports from a single source within a short window.
defense.artifacts: PowerShell script block log entries. Process Event 4688. Network: TCP SYN/RST or SYN/SYN-ACK flows for each probed port.
defense.prevention: PowerShell Constrained Language Mode (blocks New-Object). Script block logging. AppLocker policy restricting PowerShell. Network egress filter on internal-to-internal port scans.
defense.evasion: 2>$null removes exception output that might appear in transcript logs. The one-liner avoids writing a script file (fileless). Splitting the range across multiple smaller loops fragments the scanning pattern. Using the try/catch variation avoids the echo statement which is more keyword-detectable.
